title: CARDION: Webcam-Based Heart-Rate Estimation Using RGB, Simulated Events, and Spiking Neural Networks
description:
CARDION is an open-source research toolkit and local Windows application for estimating heart rate from ordinary webcam video and comparing RGB, simulated-event and neural-network approaches under a shared evaluation protocol. It combines an interactive application with source code, trained models, saved experimental results and manuscript materials so the processing methods, findings and analyses can be explored together.

Application and capabilities

The application accepts a live webcam feed, a recorded face video or a built-in simulated-face demonstration with a known pulse. It tracks facial landmarks, selects a skin region and processes changes in colour over time. A local browser interface displays estimates and guidance about measurement conditions. Video processing runs on the computer rather than being uploaded to a remote service.

  • Live camera and video-file input: examine pulse estimation from a webcam or an existing recording.
  • Built-in demo: explore the pipeline using a simulated face without a camera or dataset download.
  • Parallel comparisons: inspect conventional RGB estimators alongside classical simulated-event estimators, an artificial neural network (ANN) and a spiking neural network (SNN).
  • Reliability checks: display a reading when signal-quality, estimator-agreement and application checks pass, with guidance when a reading is withheld.
  • Validation mode: compare readings with a reference monitor and examine availability as well as error.
  • Reproduction tools: inspect saved outputs, regenerate statistical analyses and rebuild the manuscript, or rerun experiments after obtaining the original dataset separately.

The headline heart rate is produced by a gated consensus of classical RGB estimators. Event, ANN and SNN estimates are comparison outputs and do not determine that headline value. Live-camera input is a supported software feature; its accuracy has not been established by a formal live-webcam study.

Processing methods

RGB processing. MediaPipe face landmarks define a skin region excluding the eyes, brows and lips. Mean red, green and blue values form time series for green-channel, CHROM and plane-orthogonal-to-skin (POS) estimators. Filtering and spectral analysis recover a candidate pulse rhythm. Heart rate is estimated over 10-second windows with a 1-second stride. Sub-harmonic summation helps reduce selection of a harmonic instead of the underlying pulse frequency.

Event emulation. An analytic dynamic-vision-sensor emulator converts changes in log intensity into ON/OFF events. It includes contrast-threshold mismatch, refractory behaviour, leak and shot noise, with an event-rate cross-check against v2e. Three contrast thresholds, 0.02, 0.05 and 0.1, are evaluated. Events from each colour channel are grouped into 33.3-millisecond frames and processed by classical event estimators or learned pulse regressors. All events originate from compressed RGB video; no physical event camera is used.

Matched neural networks. The ANN and SNN share a layer structure and 18,289-parameter size. Hidden units use ReLU activations in the ANN or leaky integrate-and-fire neurons in the SNN, with a shared form of non-spiking readout. Both learn pulse waveforms using finger PPG as the training reference. Training uses three random seeds per threshold, and settings are selected on validation subjects.

Reliability gate. The RGB consensus requires sufficiently strong spectral peaks and agreement between at least two estimators. The frozen research rule uses a peak-ratio threshold of 8 and agreement within 8 BPM. The application adds checks for tracking duration, face count, motion and lighting. Withholding difficult windows creates an accuracy-availability trade-off: displayed readings can have lower error while measurements become less frequent.

Benchmark design

The main experiments use 60 MCD-rPPG participants, with frontal webcam recordings at rest and after exercise and synchronised finger PPG. Subjects are divided into 36 training, 12 validation and 12 test participants; recordings from the same person stay in one split. The recordings are compressed MPEG-4 video with effective frame rates of approximately 18-30 frames per second. SCAMPS examples and synthetic faces are diagnostics rather than additional real-human benchmark evidence.

Model, threshold, checkpoint and gate choices are fixed using training and validation data. Main comparisons average errors within subjects and, for networks, across training seeds. Confidence intervals are bootstrapped over the 12 test subjects; paired comparisons use Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm correction. Pooled-window agreement statistics are descriptive because overlapping windows from one person are not independent observations.

Main findings

The validation-selected methods achieved the following subject-level test mean absolute errors (MAE). Lower values indicate smaller average errors.

EstimatorTest MAE
RGB POS5.78 BPM
Classical simulated-event POS, threshold 0.0216.07 BPM
ANN on simulated events, threshold 0.0512.82 BPM
SNN on simulated events, threshold 0.118.89 BPM

RGB POS had the lowest observed error among these methods; its approximate 95% subject-bootstrap interval was 2.55-10.10 BPM. The SNN showed no accuracy advantage over the matched ANN. These findings concern the tested methods, architecture and dataset. They do not establish that pulse information is absent from simulated events or that every event-based or spiking method would perform poorly.

Displayed accuracy and availability. The gated RGB consensus achieved 2.37 BPM MAE while displaying a reading for 486 of 1,198 eligible test windows, approximately 41%. Availability ranged from 3% to 72% across test subjects. POS alone achieved 1.46 BPM on exactly those selected windows. Much of the apparent improvement over ungated results therefore comes from selecting easier windows. The gated figure describes displayed readings and should be read together with coverage; its aggregation differs from the subject-level comparison table.

Efficiency. Energy figures are operation-count proxies rather than measured electrical power. The SNN's synaptic-operation cost increases with event density and exceeds the dense ANN's operation count at fine thresholds. A coarser threshold lowers its estimated energy without providing an accuracy advantage. The proxy excludes memory traffic, neuron-state updates and sensor power and cannot establish performance on neuromorphic hardware.

Signal diagnostics. Analyses and controlled simulations identify compression, lighting flicker and weak pulse-related intensity changes as plausible contributors to the simulated-event accuracy gap. Uncompressed versions of the same recordings were unavailable, so these remain hypotheses rather than demonstrated explanations for that dataset.

Release contents and reproduction

Version 1.0.0 contains application and research source code, configuration and dependency lists, trained ANN/SNN checkpoints, subject-disjoint split manifests and checksums, saved per-window results, analysis scripts, figures and tables, automated tests, and manuscript PDF and sources. The accompanying paper is Does Event Emulation Preserve the Pulse? Frame-Based, Simulated-Event and Spiking Heart-Rate Estimators on Real Webcam Video.

On Windows, extract the archive and run Launch CARDION.bat. Initial setup installs dependencies and downloads the MediaPipe face model separately. The built-in demo offers a first exploration without a webcam. README.md, docs/USER_GUIDE.md and REPRODUCE.md explain installation, use and reproduction workflows.

Saved statistics can be checked without downloading the original videos. A claim registry links reported numbers to stored outputs, and an independent analysis script recomputes headline statistics. Rebuilding the PDF requires LaTeX. Rerunning the complete experiments requires the original dataset, approximately 7 GB of downloads and an estimated 8-12 hours on a laptop CPU; it reproduces an existing experiment rather than providing a fresh confirmatory test.

Source repository: github.com/mullenjacob/CARDION. The Zenodo archive preserves the published v1.0.0 release; the GitHub repository provides a browsable source tree and a place for subsequent development.

Scope, limitations and transparency

CARDION is a research prototype and is not a medical device. The paper is a preprint and has not been peer reviewed. Evidence is limited to one real-human dataset, 12 test subjects, one small network architecture and a limited training budget. Clinical performance, demographic fairness, accuracy during substantial motion or difficult lighting, and formal live-webcam accuracy have not been established. Simulated-event results do not establish physical event-camera performance.

The manuscript and docs/TEST_SPLIT_HISTORY.md document that the frozen models were evaluated twice to correct a summary-reporting bug; per-window predictions did not change. Later gate audits and descriptive analyses reused saved test outputs and are marked exploratory. AI coding assistance was used for substantial portions of implementation, experiment execution, analysis, literature search and initial drafting; details appear in the manuscript's Declarations.
